'''Alexander "Sasha" Arkadyevich Migdal''' ({{langx|ru|Александр Арка́дьевич Мигдал}}; born 22 July 1945) is a Russian-American mathematical and theoretical physicist currently working at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton,  New Jersey]].<ref name="ias-profile">{{cite web |author=Institute for Advanced Study |title=Alexander Migdal |url=https://www.ias.edu/scholars/alexander-migdal |website=Institute for Advanced Study|date=22 January 2024 |access-date=21 October 2026}}</ref> He is known for the Makeenko–Migdal loop equation, an exact equation for [[Wilson loop]]s in [[quantum chromodynamics]] with a large number of colors, which has been a basis for studies of [[color confinement|quark confinement]].<ref name="mm-1979">{{cite journal |last1=Makeenko |first1=Yu. M. |last2=Migdal |first2=A. A. |title=Exact Equation for the Loop Average in Multicolor QCD |journal=Physics Letters B |date=December 1979 |volume=88 |issue=1–2 |pages=135–137 |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(79)90131-X |bibcode=1979PhLB...88..135M }}</ref><ref name="mm-1981">{{cite journal |last1=Makeenko |first1=Yu. M. |last2=Migdal |first2=A. A. |title=Quantum Chromodynamics as Dynamics of Loops |journal=Nuclear Physics B |volume=188 |issue=2 |year=1981 |pages=269–316 |doi=10.1016/0550-3213(81)90105-2 |doi-broken-date=29 October 2026 }}</ref>

== Early life and education ==

Alexander Migdal was born in [[Moscow]], [[Soviet Union]] in 1945, the son of prominent Soviet physicist [[Arkady Migdal]].<ref name="paradise-lost">{{cite web |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |title=Paradise Lost |url=https://alexandermigdal.com/paradise-lost/ |website=alexandermigdal.com|access-date=21 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="rychkov-2025">{{cite journal |last=Rychkov |first=Slava |year=2025 |title=Conformal bootstrap: From Polyakov to our times |journal=International Journal of Modern Physics A |volume=40 |issue=34 |article-number=2530021 |doi=10.1142/S0217751X25300212 |arxiv=2509.02779 |bibcode=2025IJMPA..4030021R }}</ref><ref name="mononews">{{cite web |title=Мигдал, Александр Аркадьевич |url=https://mononews.ru/Мигдал,_Александр_Аркадьевич |website=mononews.ru |language=ru|access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="wework-2016">{{cite web |last=Sullivan |first=Mark |date=18 October 2016 |title=40 over 40: Physicist Sasha Migdal applies his skills to 'real life' |url=https://www.wework.com/ideas/community-stories/member-spotlight/40-40-physicist-sasha-migdal-want-apply-skills-real-life |website=WeWork Ideas |access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref>

Migdal studied physics and mathematics as an undergraduate at [[Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology]] before receiving his PhD in [[theoretical physics]] from the [[Landau Institute for Theoretical Physics]] in 1969.<ref name="ias-profile" /> He defended his doctoral degree ([[Doctor of Sciences]]) at the Landau Institute in 1973, according to his website.<ref name="paradise-lost" />

In a 2003 interview, [[Alexander Markovich Polyakov|Alexander Polyakov]] recalled that when he entered the institute, at the age of 15, he and Migdal passed the first of [[Lev Landau]]'s examinations, which he said was the mathematics examination, and that this was the only occasion on which he met Landau, shortly before Landau's accident.<ref name="polyakov-interview">{{cite web |last1=Ashrafi |first1=Babak |last2=Schweber |first2=Sam |date=6 February 2003 |title=Interview with Alexander Polyakov |url=https://authors.library.caltech.edu/5456/1/hrst.mit.edu/hrs/renormalization/Polyakov/index.html |website=Physics of Scale Activities |location=Princeton, New Jersey |access-date=21 October 2026}}</ref> Migdal has given a similar account, placing the examination in the spring of 1961, after he and Polyakov had shared first prize in a mathematical olympiad, and describing it as the first step of the "Theoretical Minimum" examination system of Landau's school.<ref name="paradise-lost" />

Migdal left the Soviet Union in 1988.<ref name="paradise-lost" />

== Career ==

Alexander Migdal began his academic career as a researcher in theoretical physics at the Landau Institute, which he joined in 1969.<ref name="paradise-lost" />

Migdal has stated that his last international symposium was in 1976, after which he was approached by the [[KGB]] and rejected its offer.<ref name="paradise-lost" />

Following his departure from the Soviet Union, Migdal spent a year at the [[University of California, San Diego]], and in 1989 joined [[Princeton University]] as a joint professor of physics and of applied and computational mathematics, according to a 2000 profile in ''U.S. 1 Newspaper''.<ref name="us1-2000">{{cite news |title=From Russia, With Love and Determination: Part I |newspaper=U.S. 1 Newspaper |location=Princeton, New Jersey |date=19 April 2000 |url=https://princetoninfo.com/from-russia-with-love-and-determination-part-i |access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref> Princeton's Office of the Dean of the Faculty, in its biography of Alexander Polyakov, likewise states that Polyakov joined the physics department in 1989 and that Migdal joined the department that year as well.<ref name="princeton-dof">{{cite web |title=Alexander Polyakov |url=https://dof.princeton.edu/people/alexander-polyakov |website=Office of the Dean of the Faculty, Princeton University|access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref> Migdal remained at Princeton until 1996, when he left to found [[Real Time Geometry]], a developer of three-dimensional [[laser scanning]].<ref name="wework-2016" /><ref name="icts-lecture">{{cite web |title=Exact Solution Of Decaying Turbulence |url=https://www.icts.res.in/lectures/ESDT |website=ICTS-TIFR|publisher=International Centre for Theoretical Sciences |access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="wsj-1997">{{Cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB862347500209275000|title=Ex-Soviet Scientist Aims To Reshape 3-D Graphics|first=David |last=Bank |date=  April 30, 1997   |newspaper=  The Wall Street Journal |url-access=subscription}}</ref>

According to ''U.S. 1 Newspaper'', Real Time Geometry was founded in 1996 by Migdal and Bob Rice, opened in Princeton that year, and was sold in December 1996 to MetaTools, a Santa Barbara software company.<ref name="us1-2000" /> A 1997 report described it as a Princeton University spin-off founded by Migdal, and the company's patent filings date from 1996;<ref name="thes-1997">{{cite news |title=Three points to a perfect image |work=Times Higher Education |date=13 June 1997 |url=https://www.timeshighereducation.com/news/three-points-to-a-perfect-image/100365.article |access-date=21 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="ep0888693">{{cite web |last1=Migdal |first1=Alexander A. |last2=Lebedev |first2=Alexei L. |last3=Petrov |first3=Michael |date=7 January 1999 |title=System and method for rapid shape digitizing and adaptive mesh generation |url=https://data.epo.org/publication-server/rest/v1.2/patents/EP0888693NWA1/document.html |website=European Patent Office|access-date=21 October 2026}}</ref> a ''Macworld'' chronology likewise dates the acquisition to 1996. In 1997 MetaTools merged with Fractal Design and other firms to form [[MetaCreations]], and MetaStream, a three-dimensional streaming format for the Web, was derived from Real Time Geometry's technology.<ref name="macworld-1999">{{cite magazine |last=Beale |first=Stephen |date=30 November 1999 |title=MetaCreations' Puzzling Move|magazine=Macworld |url=https://www.macworld.com/article/159589/15metacreations.html |access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref> Migdal continued to work at MetaCreations, and in 1999 he was a co-author of a conference paper on MetaStream.<ref name="vrml99">{{cite web |title=VRML99: Call for Participation (23–26 February 1999, Paderborn, Germany) |url=https://old.rhizome.org/community/41337/ |website=Rhizome archive|access-date=21 October 2026}}</ref> A Web 3D newsletter reported in November 1999 that ''Popular Science'' had named MetaStream a winner of its 1999 "Best of What's New" award, and ''U.S. 1 Newspaper'' reported in 2000 that the previous year's version of the software had won the award.<ref name="us1-2000" /><ref name="web3d-1999">{{cite web |last=Ressler |first=Sandy |date=10 November 1999 |title=3D Photography to the Web |url=https://www.sandyressler.com/about/library/weekly/aa111099.htm |website=Web3D Weekly (sandyressler.com) |access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref> A WeWork profile describes the award-winning tool as one for zooming, panning and rotating three-dimensional images in a web browser.<ref name="wework-2016" />

Migdal is named as an inventor on at least twelve granted United States patents assigned to Real-Time Geometry Corporation or, for later filings, to Viewpoint Corporation. They cover laser-stripe three-dimensional scanning systems, the construction of mesh models of three-dimensional objects, and the compression and transmission of moving-picture data, with filings dating from 1996 to 2000.<ref name="justia">{{cite web |title=Patents by Inventor Alexander A. Migdal |url=https://patents.justia.com/inventor/alexander-a-migdal |website=Justia Patents|access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="us5870220">{{cite web |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |title=Portable 3-D scanning system and method for rapid shape digitizing and adaptive mesh generation |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US5870220 |website=Google Patents|access-date=21 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="us5886702">{{cite web |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |title=System and method for computer modeling of 3D objects or surfaces by mesh constructions having optimal quality characteristics and dynamic resolution capabilities |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US5886702 |website=Google Patents|access-date=21 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="us6208347">{{cite web |last=Migdal |first=Alexander A. |title=System and method for computer modeling of 3D objects and 2D images by mesh constructions that incorporate non-spatial data such as color or texture |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US6208347 |website=Google Patents|access-date=21 October 2026}}</ref> A WeWork profile gives his patent count as ten, in laser scanning and three-dimensional data compression and transmission.<ref name="wework-2016" />

In 1998 Migdal founded Tachyon Systems, a Princeton company developing software for real-time analysis of stock market data, together with Keith Danko and Ward Tomlinson.<ref name="us1-2000" /> According to his personal website, he served as vice chairman and chief scientist of a public company until March 2000, then worked for almost 20 years on a stock trading system before returning to physics.<ref name="migdal-bio">{{cite web |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |title=Bio |url=https://alexandermigdal.com/ |website=alexandermigdal.com|access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref> A 2016 WeWork profile states that Migdal started four companies in total and sold the first three, and a biography published by the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences for his 2023 lecture likewise states that he founded four companies, the latest being Migdal Research LLC, which it describes as dedicated to stock market prediction.<ref name="wework-2016" /><ref name="icts-lecture" /> A limited liability company named Migdal Research LLC was incorporated in New Jersey on 20 June 2013, according to OpenCorporates, which does not list its members.<ref name="opencorporates">{{cite web |title=MIGDAL RESEARCH LLC (company number 0400582465) |url=https://opencorporates.com/companies/us_nj/0400582465 |website=OpenCorporates|access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref> A Russian-language biography published by the Saint Petersburg teachers' association describes him as chief executive of Migdal Research LLC, which it says works on stock market forecasting, and lists Viewpoint Corp and Magic Works LLC among the companies he worked for.<ref name="eduspb">{{cite web |title=МИГДАЛ Александр Аркадьевич |url=https://www.eduspb.com/node/3205 |website=Объединение учителей Санкт-Петербурга (eduspb.com) |language=ru|access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref>

Migdal returned to academia in 2019 as a research professor at [[New York University]]; his website gives the date of the appointment as October 2019, and a University of Luxembourg biography also gives 2019.<ref name="migdal-bio" /><ref name="uni-lu">{{cite web |author=University of Luxembourg, Faculty of Science, Technology and Medicine |title=Physics Colloquium / talk by Prof. Alexander Migdal |url=https://www.uni.lu/fstm-en/events/physics-colloquium-talk-by-prof-alexander-a-migdal/ |website=FSTM events, University of Luxembourg|access-date=21 October 2026}}</ref> In March 2019 he posted the first of a series of preprints on the area law and loop equation in turbulence,<ref name="arxiv-1903-08613">{{cite arXiv |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |date=20 March 2019 |title=Universal Area Law in Turbulence |class=hep-th |eprint=1903.08613}}</ref> and in a preprint of December 2019 he acknowledged support from a [[Simons Foundation]] award at New York University.<ref name="arxiv-1912-00276">{{cite arXiv |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |date=December 2019 |title=Turbulence, String Theory and Ising Model |class=hep-th |eprint=1912.00276}}</ref> He had first studied turbulence in 1993.<ref name="arxiv-9310088">{{cite journal |last=Migdal |first=A. A. |date=October 1993 |title=Loop Equation and Area Law in Turbulence |journal=International Journal of Modern Physics A |volume=09 |issue=8 |pages=1197–1238 |doi=10.1142/S0217751X94000558 |arxiv=hep-th/9310088}}</ref>

In August 2021 ''Arab News'' reported that the [[Abu Dhabi Investment Authority]] (ADIA), the [[sovereign wealth fund]] of [[Emirate of Abu Dhabi|Abu Dhabi]] in the [[United Arab Emirates]], had appointed Migdal as one of the global heads leading the research team of its quantitative research and development group.<ref name="arabnews-2021">{{cite news |title=Top sovereign fund ADIA boosts research team with new scientist hire |newspaper=Arab News |date=31 August 2021 |url=https://www.arabnews.com/business/top-sovereign-fund-adia-boosts-research-team-with-new-scientist-hire-1920166 |access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref> He was still working there in 2022: a long review of loop equations in turbulence, published in ''Physics Reports'' in 2023, states that the project was completed while he was working at ADIA, and acknowledges support from a Simons Foundation award at New York University Abu Dhabi.<ref name="physrep-2023">{{cite journal |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |year=2023 |title=Statistical Equilibrium of Circulating Fluids |journal=Physics Reports |volume=1011 |pages=1–117 |doi=10.1016/j.physrep.2023.02.001 |arxiv=2209.12312 |bibcode=2023PhR..1011....1M }}</ref>

Migdal's 2023 papers on decaying turbulence list the Department of Physics at New York University Abu Dhabi as his affiliation,<ref name="fractal-2023">{{cite journal |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |date=12 October 2023 |title=To the Theory of Decaying Turbulence |journal=Fractal and Fractional |volume=7 |issue=10 |at=754 |doi=10.3390/fractalfract7100754 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="preprints-2023">{{cite journal |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |date=19 December 2023 |title=Dual Theory of Decaying Turbulence |website=Preprints.org|doi=10.20944/preprints202312.1357.v1 |doi-access=free }}</ref> and the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences identified him with the same institution when he lectured there in December 2023.<ref name="icts-lecture" />

Migdal joined the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] as a member in September 2024. According to the Institute's profile, he was a member of the School of Mathematics for 2024–2025 and for 2025–2026, and is a member of the School of Natural Sciences from August 2026 to July 2027. The profile lists his fields of study as quantum field theory and turbulence and states an interest in quantum chromodynamics and quantum gravity.<ref name="ias-profile" />

== Scientific work ==

Migdal has made contributions to [[quantum field theory]], [[quantum gravity]] and the study of [[turbulence]].

As undergraduates, Migdal and [[Alexander Markovich Polyakov|Alexander Polyakov]] worked on dynamical mass generation in [[Gauge theory | gauge theories]], independently of [[Robert Brout]], [[François Englert]] and [[Peter Higgs]]. Migdal has said that the discovery dates from 1964 and that their paper, ''Spontaneous Breakdown of Strong Interaction Symmetry and Absence of Massless Particles'', was rejected twice by [[Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Physics | JETP]].<ref name="paradise-lost" /> The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences' scientific background for the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics states that the two had to struggle for about a year to obtain permission to submit the paper because leading Soviet scientists of the time did not support it, that it was submitted in November 1965, and that it was completely independent of developments in the West.<ref name="nobel-2013">{{cite web |author=The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences |date=8 October 2013 |title=Scientific Background on the Nobel Prize in Physics 2013: The BEH-Mechanism, Interactions with Short Range Forces and Scalar Particles |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2013/advanced-information/ |website=NobelPrize.org |access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="brink-2014">{{cite journal |last=Brink |first=Lars |year=2014 |title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 2013: The BEH-Mechanism, Interactions with Short Range Forces and Scalar Particles |journal=Proceedings of Science |id=PoS(CORFU2014)138|url=https://pos.sissa.it/231/138/pdf |access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref> The background describes the paper as a calculation to all orders in perturbation theory, using a [[Bethe–Salpeter equation]], in a spontaneously broken non-abelian gauge model with a scalar bound state, and as an independent confirmation of the second of the two mechanisms proposed by Englert and Brout. The paper was published in 1966.<ref name="mp-1966">A. A. Migdal and A. M. Polyakov, [https://web.archive.org/web/20131203014220/http://www.jetp.ac.ru/cgi-bin/dn/e_024_01_0091.pdf "Spontaneous Breakdown of Strong Interaction Symmetry and Absence of Massless Particles"], ''Soviet Physics JETP'', July 1966. Archived 3 December 2013 at the [[Wayback Machine]].</ref><ref name="close-2012">Frank Close, [https://blog.oup.com/2012/07/frank-close-new-boson-particle-higgs-find/ "Frank Close reflects on the new boson find"], ''Oxford University Press Blog'', July 2012.</ref><ref name="cern-courier">{{cite web |title=Princeton celebrates Polyakov's 60th |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110709210059/http://cerncourier.com/cws/article/cern/29554/2 |work=CERN Courier |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110709210059/http://cerncourier.com/cws/article/cern/29554/2 |archive-date=9 July 2011 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

Between 1967 and 1973, Migdal was active primarily in the area of [[critical phenomena]] and scale invariance and [[conformal field theory]], beginning with his seminal paper from 1967<ref name="gribov-migdal-1968">V. N. Gribov and A. A. Migdal, [https://web.archive.org/web/20160304050959/http://www.jetp.ac.ru/cgi-bin/dn/e_028_04_0784.pdf "Strong Coupling in the Pomeranchuk Pole Problem"], ''Soviet Physics JETP'', October 1968. Archived 4 March 2016 at the Wayback Machine.</ref> written with [[Vladimir Gribov]] connecting critical phenomena and [[quantum field theory]]. This work was subsequently developed by Migdal<ref name="migdal-1971">{{cite journal |last=Migdal |first=A. A. |title=Conformal Invariance and Bootstrap |journal=Physics Letters B |date=December 1971 |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=386–388 |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(71)90211-5 |bibcode=1971PhLB...37..386M }}</ref> and Polyakov,<ref name="rychkov-2025" /><ref name="polyakov-1970">{{cite journal |last=Polyakov |first=A. M. |date=December 1970 |title=Conformal Symmetry Of Critical Fluctuations |journal=Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Physics Letters |volume=12 |pages=381–383 |url=https://inspirehep.net/literature/61162}}</ref> working independently, into the Migdal–Polyakov [[conformal bootstrap]], and was a precursor to the work for which [[Kenneth G. Wilson | Ken Wilson]] was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1982.<ref name="wilson-nobel">{{cite web |last=Wilson |first=K. G. |title=Nobel Lecture, 1982 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1982/wilson-lecture.pdf |website=NobelPrize.org}}</ref> The conformal bootstrap was further developed by Polyakov, [[Vyacheslav Rychkov]] and others into what is now recognized as the preferred quantitative microscopic theory for understanding critical phenomena.

Migdal's work from 1974 to 1980 was focused on [[quantum chromodynamics]], starting with a paper from 1975 in which he was first to establish how [[asymptotic freedom]] could lead to [[color confinement | quark confinement]] by employing a novel form of the [[renormalization group]].<ref name="migdal-1975">A. A. Migdal, [http://www.jetp.ac.ru/cgi-bin/dn/e_042_04_0743.pdf "Phase Transitions in Gauge and Spin Lattice Systems"], ''Soviet Physics JETP'', October 1975.</ref> This work was popularized by Ken Wilson and [[Leo Kadanoff]]<ref name="kadanoff-1976">{{cite journal |last=Kadanoff |first=Leo P. |title=Notes on Migdal's Recursion Formulas |journal=Annals of Physics |date=September 1976 |volume=100 |issue=1–2 |pages=359–394 |doi=10.1016/0003-4916(76)90066-X |bibcode=1976AnPhy.100..359K }}</ref> and later became known as the "Migdal–Kadanoff bond-moving approximation,"<ref name="biroli-schehr">{{Cite web |last1=Biroli |first1=Giulio |last2=Schehr |first2=Grégory |date=11 October 2018 |title=Migdal-Kadanoff bond moving approximation |url=https://www.phys.ens.fr/IMG/pdf/td5_migdal_kadanoff.pdf |website=École normale supérieure|access-date=9 January 2023}}</ref> with lasting application in [[solid-state physics]]. In 1979, Migdal and his student [[Yuri Makeenko]] derived an exact equation for the [[Wilson loop]] in QCD with a large number of colors (large N), now known as the Makeenko–Migdal loop equation.<ref name="mm-1979" /> Makeenko and Migdal developed it further in a 1981 paper,<ref name="mm-1981" /> and Migdal reviewed the loop equations and the 1/N expansion in 1983.<ref name="migdal-1983">{{cite journal |last=Migdal |first=A. A. |title=Loop Equations and 1/N Expansion |journal=Physics Reports |volume=102 |issue=4 |year=1983 |pages=199–290 |doi=10.1016/0370-1573(83)90076-5}}</ref> The equation is now widely used in quantum chromodynamics to study quark confinement and has been a basis for string models of QCD.<ref name="nastase-2020">{{cite book |last=Nastase |first=H. |year=2020 |chapter=The Wilson Loop and the Makeenko–Migdal Loop Equation. Order Parameters; 't Hooft Loop |title=Introduction to Quantum Field Theory |pages=465–475 |location=Cambridge |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/9781108624992 |bibcode=2020iqft.book.....N |isbn=978-1-108-49399-4}}</ref><ref name="geoqcd-1">{{cite journal |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |date=April 2026 |title=Geometric QCD I: The Hodge-Dual Surface and Quark Confinement |journal=Nuclear Physics B |volume=1025 |article-number=117380 |doi=10.1016/j.nuclphysb.2026.117380 |arxiv=2511.13688 |bibcode=2026NuPhB102517380M }}</ref> More recently, Migdal has found an asymptotic solution of this loop equation for large loop areas, which describes the confining force between a quark and an antiquark; the work was published in ''Nuclear Physics B'' in 2026.<ref name="geoqcd-1" /><ref name="geoqcd-2">{{cite journal |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |date=May 2026 |title=Geometric QCD II: The Confining Twistor String and Meson Spectrum |journal=Nuclear Physics B |volume=1026 |article-number=117424 |doi=10.1016/j.nuclphysb.2026.117424 |arxiv=2602.21129 |bibcode=2026NuPhB102617424M }}</ref>

In the 1980s, Migdal (Phys. Reports '83) applied the [[matrix theory (physics) | matrix model]] to the string topological expansion of large N QCD, then [[Vladimir A. Kazakov|Vladimir Kazakov]] and F. David found that matrix models could be applied to [[topological quantum field theories]] such as [[quantum gravity]]. Initial results obtained by Migdal in collaboration with Vladimir A. Kazakov<ref name="kazakov-migdal-1988">{{cite journal |last1=Kazakov |first1=V. A. |last2=Migdal |first2=A. A. |title=Recent Progress in the Theory of Noncritical Strings |journal=Nuclear Physics B |date=December 1988 |volume=311 |issue=1 |pages=171–190 |doi=10.1016/0550-3213(88)90146-0 |bibcode=1988NuPhB.311..171K }}</ref> showed that a triangulated planar matrix model was exactly equivalent to a continuum gravity model by Knizhnik, Polyakov and Zamolodchikov (KPZ),<ref name="kpz-1988">{{cite journal |last1=Knizhnik |first1=V. G. |last2=Polyakov |first2=A. M. |last3=Zamolodchikov |first3=A. B. |title=Fractal Structure of 2D Quantum Gravity |journal=Modern Physics Letters A |volume=3 |issue=8 |year=1988 |pages=819–826 |doi=10.1142/S0217732388000982 |bibcode=1988MPLA....3..819K }}</ref> but unlike the continuum model, it offered the path to exact solution. In collaboration with [[David Gross]], Migdal further developed this work in a widely cited paper from 1990.<ref name="gross-migdal-1990">{{cite journal |last1=Gross |first1=David J. |last2=Migdal |first2=A. A. |title=A Nonperturbative Treatment of Two-Dimensional Quantum Gravity |journal=Nuclear Physics B |date=August 1990 |volume=340 |issue=2–3 |pages=333–365 |doi=10.1016/0550-3213(90)90450-R |bibcode=1990NuPhB.340..333G }}</ref> The exact solution of 2D quantum gravity through the double-scaling limit of matrix models, which reduces it to the [[Painlevé equation]], was derived simultaneously by three independent groups: Gross and Migdal at Princeton University,<ref name="gross-migdal-1990" /> Brézin and Kazakov at the [[École Normale Supérieure]],<ref name="brezin-kazakov-1990">{{cite journal |last1=Brézin |first1=E. |last2=Kazakov |first2=V. A. |title=Exactly Solvable Field Theories of Closed Strings |journal=Physics Letters B |volume=236 |issue=2 |date=15 February 1990 |pages=144–150 |doi=10.1016/0370-2693(90)90818-Q |bibcode=1990PhLB..236..144B }}</ref> and Douglas and Shenker at Rutgers University.<ref name="douglas-shenker-1990">{{cite journal |last1=Douglas |first1=Michael R. |last2=Shenker |first2=Stephen H. |title=Strings in Less Than One Dimension |journal=Nuclear Physics B |volume=335 |issue=3 |year=1990 |pages=635–654 |doi=10.1016/0550-3213(90)90522-F |bibcode=1990NuPhB.335..635D }}</ref> [[Edward Witten]] and others later expanded and generalized the applicability of matrix models to topological field theories.

In the early 1990s, Migdal began studying the application of ideas from quantum field theory to the theory of turbulence, deriving in 1993 an exact loop equation for velocity circulation within a fluid.<ref name="arxiv-9310088" /><ref name="vortex-cells">{{cite arXiv |last=Migdal |first=A. A. |date=June 1993 |title=Turbulence as Statistics of Vortex Cells |eprint=hep-th/9306152 }}</ref> Working with [[Gregory Falkovich]], Igor Kolokolov and Vladimir V. Lebedev, he developed a description of intermittency in nonlinear systems by means of [[instanton]] solutions of the stochastic differential equations.<ref name="falkovich-1996">{{cite journal |last1=Falkovich |first1=G. |last2=Kolokolov |first2=I. |last3=Lebedev |first3=V. |last4=Migdal |first4=A. |title=Instantons and Intermittency |journal=Physical Review E |date=November 1996 |volume=54 |issue=5 |pages=4896–4907 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevE.54.4896 |pmid=9965670 |arxiv=chao-dyn/9512006 |bibcode=1996PhRvE..54.4896F }}</ref>

Migdal returned to physics research in 2019, developing his earlier work on loop equations into a new approach for solving problems involving nonlinear physical flows.<ref name="arxiv-1903-08613" /> Initially, this work focused on the problem of decaying turbulence, in which a fluid flow evolves without external forcing. In a paper published in ''Fractal and Fractional'' in October 2023, Migdal reported an infinite-dimensional manifold of exact solutions of the [[Navier–Stokes equations|Navier–Stokes]] loop equation for the Wilson loop in decaying turbulence, in dimensions greater than two.<ref name="fractal-2023" /> The Wilson loop in this context is a functional of closed contours in the fluid, built from the circulation of the velocity around the contour by analogy with the Wilson loop of gauge theory, and it obeys a linear equation in the space of loops.<ref name="rodhiya-sreenivasan">{{cite journal |last1=Rodhiya |first1=Akash |last2=Sreenivasan |first2=Katepalli R. |date=13 February 2026 |title=The asymptotic state of decaying turbulence |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences |volume=384 |issue=2325 |article-number=20250021 |doi=10.1098/rsta.2025.0021 |pmid=42531315 |arxiv=2602.12501 |bibcode=2026RSPTA.38450021R }}</ref> In the paper's later sections Migdal restricts the analysis to three-dimensional space, states that the solutions do not exist in fewer than three dimensions, and states that he has not shown that solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations with smooth initial data approach this stochastic solution.<ref name="fractal-2023" />

Migdal described the solutions as equivalent to a fractal curve in a complex space, with random steps labelled by Ising-type variables and subject to number-theoretic constraints. He proposed that this gives a dual description of strongly turbulent flow as a random geometry in a different space, which he compared to the [[AdS/CFT correspondence]] of gauge theory.<ref name="fractal-2023" /><ref name="talks-cam">{{cite web |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |date=7 November 2023 |title=To the theory of decaying turbulence |url=https://www.talks.cam.ac.uk/talk/index/207811/ |website=Isaac Newton Institute Seminar Series, Talks.cam, University of Cambridge|access-date=21 October 2026}}</ref> The comparison is an analogy drawn by the author, who also writes that the paper does not claim a full solution of the decaying turbulence problem.<ref name="fractal-2023" /> He named the discrete set of loop configurations underlying the solution the Euler ensemble, in honour of [[Leonhard Euler]], and its statistics involve [[Euler's totient function]].<ref name="arxiv-2304-13719">{{cite journal |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |year=2023 |title=To the Theory of Decaying Turbulence |journal=Fractal and Fractional |volume=7 |issue=10 |page=754 |doi=10.3390/fractalfract7100754 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2304.13719}}</ref>

In 2024, Migdal published a second paper, in ''Physics of Fluids'', in which he reformulated the Euler ensemble as a [[Markov chain]] equivalent to a quantum statistical system of fermions on a ring and derived analytic expressions for the energy spectrum and energy decay of decaying turbulence. He reported that the predictions, including an asymptotic decay of the kinetic energy as ''t''<sup>−5/4</sup>, agreed with data from grid-turbulence experiments and direct numerical simulations within about 2 percent.<ref name="pof-2024">{{cite journal |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |date=24 September 2024 |title=Quantum solution of classical turbulence: Decaying energy spectrum |journal=Physics of Fluids |volume=36 |issue=9 |article-number=095161 |doi=10.1063/5.0228660 |arxiv=2312.15470 |bibcode=2024PhFl...36i5161M }}</ref><ref name="arxiv-2312-15470">{{cite journal |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |year=2024 |title=Quantum solution of classical turbulence: Decaying energy spectrum |journal=Physics of Fluids |volume=36 |issue=9 |article-number=095161 |doi=10.1063/5.0228660 |arxiv=2312.15470 |bibcode=2024PhFl...36i5161M }}</ref> Other researchers have examined the theory since. Elia Brué and Camillo De Lellis gave a rigorous mathematical treatment of parts of Migdal's momentum loop equation in a 2025 preprint,<ref name="brue-de-lellis">{{cite journal |last1=Brué |first1=Elia |last2=De Lellis |first2=Camillo |year=2025 |title=Some rigorous remarks on Migdal's momentum loop equation |journal=Journal of Mathematical Fluid Mechanics |volume=28 |issue=3 |page=45 |doi=10.1007/s00021-026-01023-8 |arxiv=2509.18992 |bibcode=2026JMFM...28...45B }}</ref> and in a 2026 paper Akash Rodhiya and [[Katepalli Sreenivasan]] compared the theory's predictions with long direct numerical simulations. They reported close agreement for simulations initialized with a Birkhoff–Saffman low-wavenumber spectrum, but a different energy decay exponent for Loitsianskii–Kolmogorov–Batchelor initial conditions, which they took to limit the universality claimed for the energy decay.<ref name="rodhiya-sreenivasan" /> The theory has also been extended by Migdal to [[magnetohydrodynamics]].<ref name="mhd-2025">{{cite arXiv |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |year=2025 |title=Dual Theory of MHD Turbulence |class=physics.flu-dyn |eprint=2503.12682}}</ref>

On 19 December 2023, Migdal gave a lecture titled "Exact Solution of Decaying Turbulence" at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences (ICTS-TIFR) in Bengaluru. The centre lists it among its Distinguished Lectures, as part of the programme "Field Theory and Turbulence", held from 18 to 22 December 2023.<ref name="icts-lecture" /><ref name="icts-ftt">{{cite web |title=Field Theory and Turbulence |url=https://icts.res.in/discussion-meeting/ftt |website=ICTS-TIFR|publisher=International Centre for Theoretical Sciences |access-date=21 October 2026}}</ref> The lecture abstract summarizes the result published in ''Fractal and Fractional''.<ref name="icts-lecture" /> He has also presented the work at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. On 14 December 2022, while affiliated with New York University Abu Dhabi, he gave the Analysis and Mathematical Physics seminar of the School of Mathematics, titled "Classical Turbulence as Quantum Geometry".<ref name="ias-math-2022">{{cite web |author=Institute for Advanced Study, School of Mathematics |title=Classical Turbulence as Quantum Geometry |url=https://www.ias.edu/math/events/analysis-and-mathematical-physics |website=Institute for Advanced Study|date=10 November 2022 |access-date=24 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="ias-video-2022">{{cite web |author=Institute for Advanced Study |title=Classical Turbulence as Quantum Geometry |url=https://www.ias.edu/video/classical-turbulence-quantum-geometry |website=IAS video archive|date=15 December 2022 |access-date=24 October 2026}}</ref> After joining the Institute as a member, he gave the same seminar series a second talk on 5 November 2024, "Duality of Fluid Mechanics and Solution of Decaying Turbulence", in which he described the duality between the Navier–Stokes equations and a one-dimensional momentum loop equation; the Institute's event page and video archive link to a recording, which is also available on YouTube.<ref name="ias-math-2024">{{cite web |author=Institute for Advanced Study, School of Mathematics |title=Duality of Fluid Mechanics and Solution of Decaying Turbulence |url=https://www.ias.edu/math/events/analysis-and-mathematical-physics-36 |website=Institute for Advanced Study|date=9 September 2024 |access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="ias-video-2024">{{cite web |author=Institute for Advanced Study |title=Duality of Fluid Mechanics and Solution of Decaying Turbulence |url=https://www.ias.edu/video/duality-fluid-mechanics-and-solution-decaying-turbulence |website=IAS video archive|date=5 November 2024 |access-date=24 October 2026}}</ref> On 16 April 2025 he gave a talk titled "Duality of Decaying Turbulence to a Solvable String Theory" at the Physics Group Meeting of the School of Natural Sciences.<ref name="ias-video-2025">{{cite web |author=Institute for Advanced Study |title=Duality of Decaying Turbulence to a Solvable String Theory |url=https://www.ias.edu/video/duality-decaying-turbulence-solvable-string-theory |website=IAS video archive|date=16 April 2025 |access-date=24 October 2026}}</ref>

In more recent research, Migdal has applied loop calculus to the planar QCD loop equation. The first of two papers in ''Nuclear Physics B'' (April 2026) presents the solution with an area law, associated with quark confinement, in which the Wilson loop contains the exponential of the area of a Hodge-dual minimal surface,<ref name="geoqcd-1" /> and the second (May 2026) treats the confining twistor string and the meson spectrum.<ref name="geoqcd-2" /> Between 12 February and 26 March 2026 he gave a series of five lectures on the subject, "Loop Dynamics and a Geometric Solution of Planar QCD", in the School of Natural Sciences at the Institute for Advanced Study. According to the Institute's video archive, the lectures were "Loop Calculus and the Coordinate Space Dilemma" (12 February); "Momentum Loop Space and the Failure of Taylor–Magnus" (20 February); "Hodge Dual Minimal Surface and Quark Confinement" (26 February); "How to Place Majorana Fermions on this Rigid Surface to Cancel Non-planar Intersections via the Pauli Principle and Recover Asymptotically Free QCD" (12 March); and "Transitioning from Phase Space of Quark Loop to Twistor Space and Extracting the Exact Geometric Mass Spectrum via Twistor Monodromies and Catastrophe Theory" (26 March). The archive lists the first, third, fourth and fifth lectures under the Institute's "IAS Matrix Pizza Night" seminar and the second under its "IAS Informal Physics Seminar".<ref name="pizza-night">{{cite web |author=Institute for Advanced Study |title=IAS Matrix Pizza Night |url=https://www.ias.edu/video-tags/ias-matrix-pizza-night |website=Institute for Advanced Study, School of Natural Sciences|date=2 April 2026 |access-date=22 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="lecture-2">{{cite web |author=Institute for Advanced Study |title=Loop Dynamics and a Geometric Solution of Planar QCD – Lecture II: Momentum Loop Space and the Failure of Taylor–Magnus |url=https://www.ias.edu/video/loop-dynamics-and-geometric-solution-planar-qcd-lecture-ii-momentum-loop-space-and-failure |website=IAS video archive|date=24 February 2026 |access-date=24 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="lecture-3">{{cite web |author=Institute for Advanced Study |title=Loop Dynamics and a Geometric Solution of Planar QCD – Lecture III: Hodge Dual Minimal Surface and Quark Confinement |url=https://www.ias.edu/video/loop-dynamics-and-geometric-solution-planar-qcd-lecture-iii-hodge-dual-minimal-surface-and |website=IAS video archive|date=27 February 2026 |access-date=24 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="lecture-4">{{cite web |author=Institute for Advanced Study |title=Loop Dynamics and a Geometric Solution of Planar QCD – Lecture IV: How to Place Majorana Fermions on this Rigid Surface to Cancel Non-planar Intersections via the Pauli Principle and Recover Asymptotically Free QCD |url=https://www.ias.edu/video/loop-dynamics-and-geometric-solution-planar-qcd-lecture-iv-how-place-majorana-fermions-rigid |website=IAS video archive|date=13 March 2026 |access-date=24 October 2026}}</ref><ref name="lecture-5">{{cite web |author=Institute for Advanced Study |title=Loop Dynamics and a Geometric Solution of Planar QCD – Lecture V: Transitioning from Phase Space of Quark Loop to Twistor Space and Extracting the Exact Geometric Mass Spectrum via Twistor Monodromies and Catastrophe Theory |url=https://www.ias.edu/video/loop-dynamics-and-geometric-solution-planar-qcd-lecture-v-transitioning-phase-space-quark |website=IAS video archive|date=27 March 2026 |access-date=24 October 2026}}</ref> The slides of all five lectures are available as a single PDF on the Institute's website, and recordings of the third and fourth lectures are also available on YouTube.<ref name="slides-2026">{{cite web |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |year=2026 |title=Loop Dynamics and a Geometric Solution of Planar QCD |url=https://www.ias.edu/sites/default/files/IASQCDLectures.pdf |website=Institute for Advanced Study|access-date=24 October 2026}}</ref>

On 27 April 2026, Migdal gave the Physics Colloquium of the University of Luxembourg, titled "Decoding fluid chaos: The arithmetic attractor of decaying turbulence". In the abstract, Migdal describes an exact decaying solution in terms of a one-dimensional momentum loop whose support is organized by reduced rational numbers, with intermittency encoded in the [[Farey sequence]], and states that recent numerical simulations support the view that the Euler ensemble describes a universal late-time state of decaying turbulence. The university's biography of the speaker describes the work as connecting classical turbulence, quantum mechanics and number theory.<ref name="uni-lu" /> In a 2026 preprint, "Reduction of Decaying Navier–Stokes Turbulence to the Quantum Pendulum", Migdal writes the Euler ensemble as a quantum trace over fermions on a ring and reduces it to an integrable system, the quantum pendulum.<ref name="arxiv-2607-05745">{{cite arXiv |last=Migdal |first=Alexander |year=2026 |title=Reduction of Decaying Navier–Stokes Turbulence to the Quantum Pendulum |class=nlin.CD |eprint=2607.05745}}</ref> The paper was available as a preprint at the time of writing.
